1.point: Open with Musa seeking Khidr, recall that the law marks the road's edge, and announce that the chapter shows why a guide helps and how to recognise a true one.
steps: A prophet who spoke with God still travelled far to be taught by a servant with knowledge from God.
So a seeker on the road to God can look for the same kind of help; the law (earlier ground) is the road's boundary, the guide is who walks it with him.
State what the chapter will establish: why a guide helps and how to know a true one.

2.point: The traveller needs a companion who has himself passed through the soul's states, whether scholars put that need at the start or later on.
steps: The road has turns inside the soul that arrive without explanation and can lose a traveller.
Only someone who has passed through those states can read them, so the guide must have travelled, not just studied.
Scholars differ on when the need begins: Bahmanpour (after the law; a beginner needs only a teacher of practice), Tabatabaʾi (at the beginning, until the higher stations), Mutahhari (at every stage).
Whatever the timing, the guide's function is the same: to read states the traveller has not yet reached, so he must have travelled.

3.point: A Shia guide holds no chain of authority of his own; he stands beneath the Prophet and Imams, and the traveller owes him submission only if he has reached a very high rank.
steps: Sufi orders answer the authority question with a silsila through which the Prophet's inner knowledge passed master to master.
Shia hold that knowledge passed by inheritance to the Imams, so there is no tariqa in Shia.
Orders demand total submission to the shaykh; Shia travellers instead find a trusted instructor from no order with no licence.
That instructor is Tabatabaʾi's general teacher, consulted as one consults anyone learned.
Submission, as opposed to consultation, requires the teacher to have reached the rank of the revelations of the Essence.
The special teachers, the Prophet and Imams, are never dispensed with, at any stage or after the end; hence the guide is under them, not in their place.

4.point: There really are such guides: Tabatabaʾi's own line of teachers, scholars and jurists reaching back to Akhund Hamadani, who taught this road and belonged to no Sufi order.
steps: If travellers must find instructors, there must be some to find; Tabatabaʾi names his, Qadi.
Qadi's line runs back to Akhund Hamadani, who trained several guides.
These men were scholars and jurists and, in Tabatabaʾi's words, belonged to no order.
They taught the road this book describes, the way to God through the self, so they are guides of the kind Section 3 defined.

5.point: Test a guide not by learning or wonders but by three things: breaking the law rules him out, long company shows how far he has gone, and the direction he turns people shows whether he is true.
steps: A guide must be tested; his learning cannot show whether he has travelled.
Wonders cannot show it either; they come early and are no sign of being a friend of God.
Abandoning one injunction of the law marks a claimant as a liar, whatever his wonders.
Keeping the law does not show how far he has gone; only long company in public and private does.
The road has pretenders who turn people to themselves; the test is whether a guide turns people to God or to himself (illustrated by ʿIsa's three marks).
Conclusion: a guide helps if tested by these means.

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: Supplies the hook: Musa, a prophet, travels far to be taught by Khidr. Nothing earlier does this.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Draws the lesson from the verse, recalls earlier ground (the law as boundary) in one sentence, and states what the chapter will establish. Does the section's whole job.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Supplies step one: the road's turns are states of the soul that arrive unexplained and can lose the traveller.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Supplies step two: only one who has passed through those states can read them, so the guide must have travelled the road. This is the core of the section's point.

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: Introduces the scholarly disagreement on timing and gives the first account (Bahmanpour: law first, guide after). The point's 'wherever scholars place the need' needs this.

¶6.label: support
¶6.why: Completes Bahmanpour's account by saying what a beginner does need instead (a teacher of practice), with Qadi's Musabbihat year as the example; ¶17 later refers back to it. Weak: the Musabbihat detail is more than the step needs.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Second account (Tabatabaʾi: at the beginning, until higher stations). Also introduces the general/special teacher distinction that Section 3 builds on.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: Third account (Mutahhari: every stage), completing the announced range, and supplies the Khidr couplet ¶9 uses.

¶9.label: restate
¶9.why: Its main claim, that the guide must have travelled the road to read states, is ¶4's claim; the rest summarises ¶5-¶8. The link could be one sentence at the end of ¶8.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: Poses the authority question and gives the Sufi answer: tariqa, elder, silsila back to the Prophet through which inner knowledge passed.

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: Gives the Shia answer: the knowledge passed by inheritance to the Imams, hence no tariqa in Shia. Supplies the 'under the Imams' half of the point.

¶12.label: advance
¶12.why: Contrasts the orders' total submission with the Shia practice of finding a trusted instructor from no order. Sets up the question of what submission such an instructor is owed.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Places the Shia instructor as Tabatabaʾi's general teacher, consulted like anyone learned. Needed to apply Tabatabaʾi's bar in ¶14.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Supplies the high bar for submission: consultation is open, submission only to one in whom the revelations of the Essence are manifest. The second half of the point.

¶15.label: advance
¶15.why: Defines the special teacher as the Prophet and Imams whose inner company is never dispensed with. This is what puts the guide 'under' them and 'never in their place'.

¶16.label: restate
¶16.why: Combines ¶11, ¶14 and ¶15 into a summary; no new link. The forward pointer to Chapter Fifteen is housekeeping, not argument.

¶17.label: advance
¶17.why: Opens the existence question and names the first guide: Tabatabaʾi's own teacher Qadi, tied back to ¶6.

¶18.label: advance
¶18.why: Extends the line two generations to Akhund Hamadani and shows he trained several guides. Needed for 'a line' and 'recent generations'. The disambiguation from the other Hamadani is a brief necessary aside within it.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Supplies the second half of the point: these were scholars and jurists and, in Tabatabaʾi's words, belonged to no order.

¶20.label: aside
¶20.why: Raises a puzzle the chapter itself creates (Tabatabaʾi calls his line a tariqah) and resolves it. If cut, no later sentence breaks and ¶19 already carries the 'no order' step. At most a one-sentence note in ¶19.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Shows the line taught the road this book describes (knowledge of the self), which makes them guides 'of this kind' rather than just named scholars. Its last sentence states the point once.

¶22.label: advance
¶22.why: Supplies why a test is needed and the first negative: learning cannot show whether a teacher has travelled.

¶23.label: advance
¶23.why: Second negative: wonders cannot show it, they come early and are no sign of being a wali. Supplies the point's 'never by wonders'.

¶24.label: advance
¶24.why: First positive test: breaking one injunction marks a claimant a liar, whatever his wonders. Supplies 'a guide who breaks the law is ruled out'.

¶25.label: advance
¶25.why: Second positive test: the law only rules out; long company in public and private shows how far a true guide has gone. Supplies 'shown by long company'.

¶26.label: support
¶26.why: Applies the law test to the case where long company is impossible: weigh his prescriptions against the Book, Sunnah and Imams. ¶27's 'either way' depends on it. Not named in the point, so the weakest support.

¶27.label: advance
¶27.why: Third positive test: pretenders turn people to themselves; a true guide turns them to God. Supplies 'recognised by where he turns people'.

¶28.label: support
¶28.why: Introduces the ʿIsa saying as the simplest form of the direction test; exists only to set up the quotation that ¶29 uses. Thin, but ¶29 would be unanchored without it.

¶29.label: support
¶29.why: Reads the quotation: the three marks all ask where a person's company turns us, and they can be watched over time. Ties the ʿIsa evidence to the tests in ¶27 and ¶25.

¶30.label: restate
¶30.why: Summarises the whole chapter: travelled the road (¶4), under the Imams (¶15-16), wonders prove nothing (¶23), law rules out (¶24), long company (¶25), direction (¶27). Every claim already stated, several of them twice.

¶31.label: aside
¶31.why: A bridging question to the next chapter; adds no link to this section's point and raises a question the chapter does not answer.
